utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Xinyue Wang, who is from the People's Republic of China and who has been assisting my team for a month. She's a master's student at the University of Groningen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. I didn't remember that Judge Morrison couldn't be with us due to his medical appointment which could not be moved. So therefore we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis for today. Yes, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it next witness is Mr. Kondic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we rise until 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if he hasn't -- if he's not here yet then we should do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise. --- Break taken at 9.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kondic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Minister. I am afraid that the microphone does not register nodding, so you have to say everything that you want to have recorded here.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, I kindly ask you to pause between my questions and your answers so that all of them could be recorded in the transcript. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement to a representative of your team. I think it was the beginning of this year, something around then. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D9521 in e-court so that the witness could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the statement on the screen, but I also have a hard copy and I've been allowed to use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just pause a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I stated what I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is recorded as you had put it; right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today live, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I hope they would be the same. Of course one cannot phrase one's sentences identically, but the answers would be the same. I spoke about what I remembered and there's a time distance involved, 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how about the associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are 16 associated exhibits. The Prosecution has pointed out some problems with two of them, so we won't be tendering 1D9189, which is an article from "Glas" magazine for which we had the English translation but no original; and we also won't be tendering 05437, which is a document that didn't contain an English translation, the quote from the article that was in Serbian but we don't want to take the time to lead that live. So we'll withdraw those two and we persist with the other 14. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the admission of the statement as well as 14 associated exhibits, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honour. I have one objection regarding the statement which is to paragraph 35, which the Prosecution contends is tu quoque evidence regarding the electricity situation in the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thirty-five?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "... Krajina area had power only two hours every 20 days. The situation was very difficult for all citizens." And your argument is that is tu quoque?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This appears to be part of the same argument which is that there were difficult conditions for citizens or civilians in Bosnian Serb-held territory. I would further add that the statement at this paragraph refers to a Prosecution exhibit, Exhibit 3104, but I would add that that document only refers to at page 6 of the English and pages 5 to 6 of the B/C/S, financing an investment relating to repairing and installing electricity in the Krajina region. So it doesn't seem that this Prosecution exhibit relates to the comment here, which is simply that the Krajina area had power for two hours every 20 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from the issue whether this may be relevant or not, I'm not following how this is a tu quoque argument which -- regarding the power, electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The times that we've seen this argument in the past, Your Honour, it has been raised in the context of evidence that the Prosecution has presented showing deprivations of electricity, particularly in the Sarajevo area as part of the efforts by the Bosnian Serb leadership to increase or decrease tensions in the Sarajevo area by using utilities as a means to that end. And we've heard through various other witnesses examples of testimony relating to electricity outages in other parts of the country in Bosnian Serb-held territory, and that seems to be the only reason for advancing this claim. Otherwise, this doesn't seem to be relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Chamber is not persuaded by your argument, Mr. File. The statement will be admitted in its entirety together with 14 associated exhibits. Shall we give -- assign the number for the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4063, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The exhibit numbers for the associated exhibits will be assigned in due course by the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Novak Kondic's statement. [In English] Novak Kondic was a member of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff. Also, he was in charge of the monetary politics [sic] of the municipality of Banja Luka. He became a member of the SDS in 1994. Before the war, Novak Kondic worked at the public auditing service which kept accounts of all legal entities in Banja Luka and ensured the legality of all their operations and carried out transactions for the SFRY and collected and distributed cash for banks and post offices. Novak Kondic considers that public opinion in BH was under great pressure following the events in Croatia, and everyone was fearful and this caused the mass exodus of Serbs from Croatia at the beginning of the war in Croatia. The people of Banja Luka took refugees into their homes to give them food and wash. There was a mix of ethnicities amongst the refugees. The SDS was established after the SDA and HDZ as a response to the other two parties. There is no basis whatsoever to conclude that the policy of the SDS party from its establishment was the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory in BH through genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and inhumane acts. The SDS created organs of authority and were respected. Everyone was aware of the establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH and it occurred as a response to the attempts of the anti-constitutional independence of BH and its secession from the SFRY. As a member of the Crisis Staff, Novak Kondic was aware that following the only meeting of the Crisis Staff, the aim of the Crisis Staff was to ensure more or less normal life for the people of the municipality with regard to the supply of water, electricity, tax, funding for schools, healthcare, and everything that could be ensured. Novak Kondic does not consider that the Crisis Staffs in municipalities served as a vehicle for the permanent removal of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory through genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and inhumane acts. There was only one session of the War Presidency of Banja Luka municipality held before its functions were taken over by the ARK Crisis Staff. In April 1992, following armed clashes in Sarajevo, the regular application of laws ceased and the municipalities discussed how to organise the functioning of the economic and financial system. The Autonomous Region of Krajina was created and the statute was modelled on the statute of the BH public auditing service. The ARK quickly established a financial system that was integrated with other regional systems. All work done in relation to the payments system was entirely according to the laws of the SFRY and BH. In relation to financing the ARK, expenses were paid from the municipal budgets as there was no regulation for them collecting funds. The fund for defence of the ARK was established to finance the basic needs of the army, including toiletries, clothing, and food. No irregularities were noted in the fund. The healthcare, pension, employment and other funds were operated at the level of the ARK and funds were autonomous from the republican organs in Pale until the establishment of a unified system. All employees paid a certain amount of their salaries into special funds. Until the unified payment system was established in 1992 and 1993, the ARK did not fund the activities of the Republika Srpska. Civilians in Banja Luka were allowed to take foreign currency out of the ARK territory. The regulations were based on the pre-war federal law. The provisions applied to everyone no matter what their ethnic background. Novak Kondic considers that from September 1992 onwards the ARK slowly began to be abolished. From his position on the Executive Board, Novak Kondic is aware that the position of the Banja Luka Executive Board were divided according to the inter-party agreement. In September 1993, Novak Kondic, along with other member of the Executive Board, were interrogated by the armed men. He still does not understand why. Novak Kondic is aware that for at least two years in Krajina area had power for only two hours every 20 days. The situation was very difficult for all citizens. And that is a short summary, and at that moment I do not have additional questions for Mr. Kondic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just suggest something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kondic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first sentence you said that I was in charge of monetary policy, whereas in actual fact I was in charge of the system of payments and monetary policy was within the national bank of Republika Srpska, so just that, to make a distinction between the two, because they're separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, this is not evidence. This is just a summary of your statement and obviously it is not very precise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. As you have noted, Mr. Kondic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kondic. In your statement you said that you were not a member of the SDS party until 1994 and that you "don't know anything about leadership in the party and other organs." Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were never part of the SDS party leadership at any level, were you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you did not participate in any meetings of the SDS party leadership?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You didn't attend any RS Assembly sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I attended RS Assembly sessions as director for the payment system where our reports on payment transactions in the payment system were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Did you participate in any way in formulating SDS party policies?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 of your statement you say: "There is no basis whatsoever to conclude that the policy of the SDS party in the period from the establishment of the party on 12 July 1992 onward was the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory in BH through genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and inhumane acts (forcible transfer). I have never heard that there was a desire to exterminate or deport anyone ..." So based on what we've just discussed, this is not coming from your personal experience in the SDS; this is just what you believe. Is that a fair summary of your position?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I would say that at the time there was fear in every person after everything that had happened in Croatia when columns of refugees were coming into Banja Luka. I think as an ordinary citizen that we considered the SDS to be a movement and protection from a breakout of war and everything that was already going on in Croatia. So I was speaking about that as an ordinary citizen in terms of how I viewed the situation then because that is how all people saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were a member of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your statement you said that only one session of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff was ever called, or at least you were only given notice of one session. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. Actually, I was the director of the tax department of the municipality of Banja Luka and the Crisis Staff was made up of persons who were in charge of particular sectors within the municipality. This session was convened. As far as I can remember, what was discussed there was creating conditions for the functioning of normal civilian life in town. Of course after this one session, I was never asked to come again - perhaps they weren't held anymore - and it was the president of the municipality, Mr. Predrag Radic, that chaired the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, you were also a member of the Banja Luka War Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No. The Crisis Staff of the city of Banja Luka. It was no War Presidency. I don't know of the existence of any War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could I refer you to paragraph 33 of your statement. I'm going to read what you said in that paragraph. You said: "I have been shown document 1D25042. This is a decision appointing me to the War Presidency of Banja Luka. Only one session of this War Presidency of the Banja Luka municipality was held on 6 May 1992, but this function was taken over by the ARK KS" Crisis Staff "immediately after this session ..." So you were a member of a War Presidency that met on one occasion; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No, sorry, that's a mistake in the term that was used because it was explained in paragraph 8, that's the Crisis Staff that I spoke of. It's not the War Presidency. So I think that this was just misstated, that I misspoke actually. War Presidency, I don't even know of its existence and I was not a member of a War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the top of this document, we're referring to 1D25042, this is a document from the Banja Luka municipality Executive Committee. It's dated at the top 5 September 1991, although in your statement at paragraph 33 you said that the date written in the document was wrong. And if you go to where it says "decision," it indicates this is a decision on establishing the War Presidency of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly. And you were -- you'll see at number 2 -- part II, number 10, towards the bottom of the page, you'll see your name, Novak Kondic, director of the AR /Autonomous Region/ of Krajina SDK /Public Auditing Service/, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Actually, the wording is wrong. Wrong terms were used. This decision says that was a War Presidency. Under 8 I said a Crisis Staff. That was the same group of people who were appointed, but I don't know what the name of the body was previously but it's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Would you like to take a break at this point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, where do we see Crisis Staff under 8? Could you repeat, Mr. Kondic, what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that those two things were the same. I said in my paragraph 8 that that was a Crisis Staff, that was the terminology that was used; however, it is about its name being a War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you -- in paragraph 33 you mention "War Presidency," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that this document was shown to me when I was providing my statement, which is why I used the same term as in the document because it is all about this document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you stated that War Presidency was taken over by the Crisis Staff. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did say -- let me explain. It is one and the same thing. I didn't see previously that according to this decision the name of that body was War Presidency. I said that a body was indeed set up, and when the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina staff did -- operating, I believe that those issues that pertained to the purview of the War Presidency were transferred on to different body or different bodies. We never met. There was that -- just that one meeting to which we were called in order to be invited to help the functioning of normal life in town, including water, electricity, tax collection, and everything else that concerned normal conditions of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 30 minutes and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Kondic, before the break we were discussing this document, 1D25042, the document that appointed you as a member of the Banja Luka War Presidency. At page 20 of today's transcript you said that the wording is wrong in that document. I want to just clarify, is it your testimony that there was not a municipal Crisis Staff in Banja Luka that existed before the Banja Luka War Presidency was established in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I only remember that one body was indeed appointed and set up. I don't know whether it was called War Presidency or Crisis Staff. If we look at this decision, those are mostly members of the Executive Council, and I was its member. This was a municipal body which was set up. I attended just one meeting of that body and no other meetings after that. I don't know if it continued operating at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: My question was whether any entity of this sort existed before this date of 6 May 1992 [sic]. Was there any Crisis Staff or any War Presidency before then?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't know. I can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter number 04 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But is it your evidence that the date is wrong on the page we are looking at now, Mr. Kondic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the date. I can see that the date has been corrected on this page, but I really do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Did you say date has been corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see in the document that the day and month are illegible, whereas the year is quite clearly legible. That's why I'm saying that I don't know, I can't remember the date. I don't know when this decision was actually passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the upper part of the document which refers to the document number, strictly confidential --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- but it still bears the number of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and you can see clearly that it was on the 5th of September, 1991; however, further down, when describing that particular session and the date when it was held, that part is not very clear or legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the parenthesis, Official Gazette of Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina number 3/92, does that number, 92, represent the year, Mr. File? Do you have any clue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, should we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could turn to 65 ter number 04998, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Kondic, you'll see that this is a newspaper article from "Glas" from the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to look at B/C/S page 2, English page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, you'll see the headline at the top of the page in B/C/S and at approximately the middle to the bottom of the page in the English says: "Crisis Staff session takes place. "SOS demands accepted." And in the first paragraph of the article it says: "Banja Luka, 3 April - at a press conference today, Predrag Radic, President of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff, declared that all of the Serbian Defence Forces' /SOS/ demands had been agreed to, true, in a slightly modified form ..." One more area of this page I'm going to draw your attention to is in the English page 6 and it's the box that is in the middle of that article in B/C/S titled "Crisis Staff." And this contains a list of individuals who were appointed to the Crisis Staff. You'll see this list does not contain your name. So my question to you is: Does this refresh your recollection as to whether a Crisis Staff existed in the month before the establishment of this War Presidency that we were discussing earlier?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I believe that it may be concluded from the document that the staff did exist; however, I know that there was one body that consisted mostly of the members of the Executive Council and I was one of the members. That was the War Presidency that had only one session and I really don't know anything else about that. Because here the -- there is a reference to the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Banja Luka. I was not a member, I don't know how it functioned, and I don't know how long it existed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But you agree that you were present in Banja Luka at the time and you were aware of the existence of this staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I suppose that I knew at the time, but that was 20 years ago. Now as I sit here, I really can't be sure. I know that there was one body, I was appointed to that body, I attended just one meeting and no meetings after that because, A, there were no such meetings; and B, I was never called to any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it -- yes, Mr. -- before that, yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would think just those two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in B/C/S is one page. Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement what you said about the meeting of this War Presidency was that it took place on the 6th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see that from the document because the document bears that date, 6th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter number 05443, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see at the top of this page, this is an excerpt from the minutes of the 69th Session of the Executive Committee of Banja Luka municipality, held on the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we go to English page 10 and B/C/S page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see under item 20 it says: "The Committee adopted a decision establishing a War Presidency of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly." So this would seem to suggest that the Banja Luka War Presidency was established on the 8th of May, 1992. Does that refresh your recollection as to the date of the establishment of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the date at all, not after the time that has lapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to disagree with what is stated in the minutes of this 69th Session of the Executive Committee of Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I believe that the minutes are credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could I tender that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second. Shall we admit it in its entirety, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or only those pages? First and last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we'd just as soon have it admitted in its entirety, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll admit those two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter number 5502, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When this comes up, you'll see that these are the abridged minutes of the 19th Session of the Assembly of the municipality of Banja Luka, dated 23 June 1992. On page 1 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S, towards the bottom, it says in the large paragraph: "The President informed Assembly members that there were no changes and amendments to the agenda, except that the War Presidency had in the meantime, from the sending of the materials to the holding of the session, on 19 June 1992 reviewed and adopted the Decision under point 3 of the agenda which says: The Draft Decision on violations at a time of imminent threat of war or in the event of war; I therefore propose that this Decision be reviewed as part of point 2 of the agenda, like all other decisions adopted by the War Presidency." And if you go to English page 2, at the bottom of B/C/S page 1, under item 2, it says: "Verification of the decisions adopted by the War Presidency of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly within the competencies of the Municipal Assembly in the period from 28 May 1992 to 23 June 1992 ..." And then going on to page 2 of the B/C/S, it has a whole list of decisions in areas that include the allocation of municipal apartments, appointing and replacing judges, and this issue of violations at a time of imminent threat of war or in the event of war. So in addition to the meeting you were previously saying happened on the 6th -- on or about the 6th of May, 1992, this seems to suggest that there were numerous meetings of the Banja Luka War Presidency between 28 May 1992 and 23 June 1992, including one that is specifically mentioned as having taken place on 19 June 1992. So would you agree, in light of this, that your recollection about the extent of these meetings could be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: It is possible, because from this I can see that the War Presidency was the Executive Council of the city of Banja Luka and I was its member. I suppose that decisions were passed at meetings of the Executive Council, which operated as the War Presidency and they were sent to the Assembly; because the Executive Council made decisions from within its regular purview and sent them for review to the Assembly and for adoption. I suppose that I may have forgotten the terminology. I don't know whether the state of war was declared and the Executive Council was renamed and became a War Presidency. I believe that that would be the explanation, but I don't know. However, when we looked at the article in "Glas," it says there that that was the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Banja Luka and I suppose that I related that activity to that -- to this one meeting of the Executive Council. If you look at the composition of the War Presidency, those were mostly members of the Executive Council and you can see their functions; i.e., you can see what sectors they covered. And it is a purely legal phrasing and a legal issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at English page 5, B/C/S page 4 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, you will see at the bottom of the page in English and in B/C/S, you were attending this session of the Assembly of the municipality of Banja Luka because you presented introductory comments to two decisions of the War Presidency relating to sales taxes. That's at the bottom of those pages. Do you recall being present for this session?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I was a member of the Executive Council and we were duty-bound to attend Assembly sessions, and you can see from the minutes that my presence was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit those pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at document 65 ter 5520, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: As this comes up, you'll see that this is a letter from the Banja Luka public prosecutor to the Banja Luka War Presidency dated 6th of July, 1992. This letter is proposing deputy public prosecutors for Banja Luka to be confirmed by the War Presidency, and in particular it says in the second paragraph: "In view of the legal provision on the Public Prosecutor's Office in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the decision on the structure of organisation, the seat and areas /that concern/ the offices of public prosecutors adopted by the acting president of the republic, the War Presidency must give its approval for the appointment of the Deputy Public Prosecutor. Please could you, therefore, approve this at the next session." Now, you would agree that this seems to indicate that other public officials viewed the Banja Luka War Presidency as functioning in July 1992 because it makes a request for approval to take place at the next session; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - and you can also see from the document - the Executive Council of the city of Banja Luka, or rather, of the municipality of Banja Luka, as it was known at the time, was renamed and became War Presidency, which means that all the functions that Executive Council performed up to April 1992, it continued to perform. But a decision had been made to rename it so that it became a War Presidency. You can see from the composition of the people who were its members. It could not have been an illegal group, a random group of people that made decisions that would then be sent to the Assembly. It's a very legal issue and I'm a layperson, but as far as I can remember that's how things were and you can see from the document that this was actually the Executive Council of the city of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So now it's your testimony that the War Presidency was sometimes -- on at least one occasion a Crisis Staff but other times it was the Executive Council; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that from this -- the documents, you can see that the Executive Council was renamed and became a War Presidency. And as for the Crisis Staff, as far as I can remember it was set up, its president was Predrag Radic, the president of the Assembly. I attended its session only once and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Before we get away from this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You don't recall attending any War Presidency sessions in July 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I know from the documents - and you can also check that with the people who were in charge of the Executive Council, its president Rajko Kasagic, for example - it arises from this that at the time the Executive Council was renamed and became a War Presidency. This is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, I noticed another comment in your statement when you said at paragraph 16: "In the ARK we acted like a separate state whose supreme organ was the ARK Assembly ..." This letter has a local prosecutor talking about meeting the requirements of republic-level legal provisions and presidential decisions that establish procedures relating to municipal War Presidencies. So you would agree that this letter is inconsistent with your claim that the highest law of the land in Krajina came from the ARK Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: It arises from this that the ARK Assembly existed for only a few months, until the moment Republika Srpska was territorially integrated. ARK Assembly passed decisions that were then sent to various institutions in the area for implementation. That was between April 1992 to September 1999 [as interpreted]. And then the National Assembly, the government, and other institutions took over and started functioning normally --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: -- and during that time the Assembly of ARK and its Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This letter comes from 6th of July, 1992, so you're limiting your claim about the ARK Assembly to before that date; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I cannot be tied to the date because I don't remember dates after all this time, but I know that at the beginning of the divisions of the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole concerning the area of Banja Luka and other municipalities, the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was formed and it took over certain legislative and other functions and functions of the Presidency and executive functions, especially in the payment system.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we just look briefly at P2620, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see this is an ARK Crisis Staff document from Radoslav Brdjanin dated 11 June 1992, and it says at the top: "On the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the municipal Crisis Staff, that is the War Presidency, shall consist of the following persons ..." And then it has a list. And then again it says: "The War Presidency, that is the Crisis Staff ..." and it explains the duties. Now, this doesn't say anything about the War Presidency being an Executive Committee, it refers specifically to the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: It is obvious from this that the Crisis Staff is, in fact, a completely different organ than the Executive Committee or the War Presidency which was in place during the war because people have different functions here, whereas on the Executive Board of the region of Banja Luka there are certain people who had been elected before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But this document creates an equivalency between the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, not between the Executive Council and the War Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No, no. The Executive Board was renamed, as we could see in that decision, into War Presidency. And the members of the War Presidency were the members of the Executive Board that had been elected to those posts. So this war -- what you call it, the War Presidency, is not related to this organ referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter number 25685, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So as you can see from this document, it's a decision of the Banja Luka War Presidency dated 7 July 1992. It says at the top: "At a session held on 7 July 1992, the War Presidency of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly adopted the following decision: "Relieving the editor-in-chief of the Banja Luka 'Glas' newspaper /of his duties/ ..." I'm going to show you one more document and then I'm going to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 25684, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And as you can see from this, this is a decision of the Banja Luka War Presidency dated 16 July 1992, and it says: "At its session of 16 July 1992, the War Presidency of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly ... adopted the following decision ..." So you see, there are sessions of the War Presidency, as its called, taking place in July 1992, but it's your testimony that there was only one session of the War Presidency; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain that there existed one body headed by the president of the municipality, Predrag Radic. I'm not sure whether it was called the War Presidency or it was called the Crisis Staff, but we see from the documents that the administrative board -- in fact, that some sort of War Presidency was formed made up mainly of members of the Executive Board and it's logical that such decisions were made by that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But the very first document that we saw today was a document that was nominating you to the War Presidency. You were a member of the War Presidency. So you didn't attend any of these meetings; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that by virtue of that decision I was named member of the Executive Board. Because look at the War Presidency, all of these people were former members of the Executive Board that had been legally elected to the Executive Board. And that body was renamed into War Presidency. On the other hand, there was the Crisis Staff, to which I was appointed, it held only one session and I was never again invited there. So you can see clearly that these are two different bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Final area of questions. In numerous places in your statement you discuss how the BiH SDK in Sarajevo cut off payment transactions with the Banja Luka SDK branch office, that's at paragraph 10 where you say that: "Payment transactions with municipalities from the Banja Luka region were cut off ..." relating to April 1992. And then again in paragraph 12 you say: "At one point the BH SDK cut payment transactions with the Banja Luka SDK branch office, but I do not remember why ..." Now, my question to you is: Are you aware that well before payment transactions with the Banja Luka SDK were cut off, the SDS leadership had issued instructions to take over power in SDK branches?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And for the record, I'm referring to Exhibits P2548 and P958.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The question is: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: In that period there was an antagonism; in fact, there were problems in the distribution of funds between the central authorities in Sarajevo and the authorities in Banja Luka. The system operated in such a way that those revenues that were collected in the area of the municipality of Banja Luka were sent every night to the centre in Sarajevo where they were to be redistributed so that part of the funds went to Belgrade in the form of federal taxes, part of the revenues remained in Sarajevo, and part in Banja Luka. There were certain major problems in returning a portion of these funds to the local level --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Kondic --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: -- so there was a dialogue between --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- pardon me for interrupting, but my question was more narrow and more specific than that. I was simply asking you whether you were aware that before the payment transactions were cut off from Sarajevo, if you were aware that the SDS leadership had issued instructions to take over power in SDK branches. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I know that certain decisions were made and that they were enacted in circumstances when the payment transaction system was paralyzed. Attempts were made to continue observing the regulations and send funds to Sarajevo; however, there were power cuts on the local level and the payments authorities were unable to process that. I know the Assembly discussed it and the president of the Assembly, Mr. Pelivan, certain decisions were made but I really can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember any -- the existence of any instructions from SDS leadership to prevent SDK branches in Serb-dominated areas from releasing money from their treasuries, effectively cutting off transactions with other parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I know that there was a series of decisions and debates primarily before the Assembly of Banja Luka and then talks ensued with the official authorities in Sarajevo, with the aim of deciding how to use the funds more regularly, more appropriately. May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Actually, if we could just look at Exhibit P5, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see that this is SDS Main Board instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions. This is the Variant A and B document from 19 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could just look at English page 5 and B/C/S page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see under "second degree," point 4, the instruction here is to: "Make the SDK /Public Accounting Services/ branch and affiliated offices responsible for preventing the physical outflow of cash and securities from the treasuries under their jurisdiction in banks, post offices, and other financial institutions ..." Now, these instructions are coming in December 1991, well before the electricity cutoffs that you were describing; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see from the document that it was issued on 19 December 1991 by the Main Board of the SDS, but of course we did not apply this because we did not apply this at that time. The unified system in Bosnia-Herzegovina was still in operation if we are talking about capital payments. This may have been some sort of recommendation, but I did not see it nor was I in a position to act upon this. Because the general director of the capital payment service was still in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: -- that was a director for payments in Banja Luka and I was the director of the tax administration in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that you didn't see these instructions?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe I had seen it then, but I really don't remember. I cannot remember all the documents or remember them after 22 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two or three questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kondic, could we look at 25684. It probably has a P number now. 65 ter 25684. Do you remember those numerous decisions? It will come up soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, did you tender those two decisions by War Presidency, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I may not have, but I intended to. If I could please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25685 receives Exhibit P6526. 65 ter number 25684 receives Exhibit P6527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could be P6523. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All those decisions that you saw in several documents, if there had been no war, in whose jurisdiction were such decisions? If it hadn't been for the war, which body would have issued those decisions?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Assembly in Sarajevo was competent to legislate, to enact certain laws; and based on those laws, municipalities were competent to issue some regulations, such as the Assembly in Banja Luka. Some of these decisions enacted by the Assembly during the war used to be enacted and issued by other bodies than the Assembly after 1992. Speaking of these decisions about collection of taxes and contributions, these decisions were enacted based on the existing laws but received a different framework before the Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who by ethnicity are Edin Hergic, Kemal Arnautovic, then Azra Viscevic, and Gordana Preselj? Who were these people on the Executive Board by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: It is unambiguous that these are Muslims and Croats. I remember some of these names, but, for instance, the vice-president of the Executive Board was Anton Rusic a Croat; Josip Cujec, Croat; and there were two Bosniaks whose names elude me at the moment, Nedzad Kusmic is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This, for instance, is the month of May, but we've seen that on 23rd June and 6th July there were other documents. Did they continue to work in the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: They continued, but, to be quite honest, I worked until September 1992 when I was appointed deputy director of the payment service and I left the Executive Board so I don't know how long they continued on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was said here that those instructions, regardless of how we treat them -- can you tell us, what was the situation with the outflow of cash among the republics and when did this new situation arise in the payment transactions among the republics?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: The problem with the distribution of revenues between local communities and republic organs became very tense on the eve of the war and there were many meetings between presidents of Municipal Assemblies and the president of the Executive Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Pelivan at the time. And those tensions culminated in great discontent. At that time I was a member of the Presidency of the League of Communists of the municipality of Banja Luka, and this discontent with the overall relations between local and republic authorities, the decision was made to stop paying the contributions, the fees, the membership fees, to the League of Communists to Sarajevo and to keep them in Banja Luka. The head of that committee was a Croat, Zvonko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that before the SDS was established?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but I believe it was before the establishment of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Staying on the same subject, what did it look like between republics and the Federation, this same problem?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: We had some information based on the tax inspections done by the SDK in Belgrade, which checked the six branch offices in the republics. And I know there were problems in the supply of cash because all the republics used to be supplied from Belgrade, from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Then there was some problems and complaints regarding the taxes payable to the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And last, what happened to the foreign exchange -- foreign currency savings of citizens of households before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: What I know as a regular citizen is that the foreign currency savings evaporated. People were unable to access their foreign currency savings accounts, and to date these problems persist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where, for instance, did the savings held by the Ljubljanska Banka in Bosnia-Herzegovina disappear?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a problem between the Bank of Republika Srpska and the National Bank of Yugoslavia. That had nothing to do with my job which was payment transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Kondic.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KONDIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Kondic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grahovac. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We both need to mind how we speak. We need to speak slowly and make a short pause between questions and answers so that everything is properly recorded. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I have given a statement to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D9520, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I have seen that statement and I signed it, but concerning paragraphs 40 and 41, I would like to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display paragraphs 40 and 41. It's page 12 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us what needs to be clarified in paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Let me see. It seems to me this record is not the last one looked at. It could be the next one, 41. Yes, 41. In the sentence that begins with: "I was also ..." That sentence should be deleted and replaced with the following: "I too could have been killed by such men on one of the bridges across the Vrbas river, like the chief of security of Banja Luka, Goran Ilic [as interpreted], was killed and he was my friend and neighbour ..." So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we see the next page, at least in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "I too ...," second line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you say "Goran Ilic" or "Goran Bjelica"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "Goran Bijelic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was that bridge that he was victimised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any other corrections you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was in my paragraph 41, but I think it is in your paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's in 41. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 42 as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would you change there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: The last name of the woman referred to there is not "Pavelic," it is "Pajic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Marinka Pajic; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be shown to the witness so he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honours, and I wouldn't normally interrupt Dr. Karadzic at this stage in the game, but since we're dealing with corrections to the statement I just wanted to bring to everybody's attention in relation to paragraphs 18 -- paragraph 18 of the statement and 17, both of those refer to quotes from a document which is already exhibited and which was referenced in the draft version of the statement. But the actual reference to the document has been deleted, and that's D4016. Paragraphs 17 and 18 actually quote that document almost entirely. So perhaps it would help things if there was just a reference to D4016 inserted somewhere in relation to those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just it might be inadvertence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Defence agrees to your statement, then that will be fine. So paragraph 17 and paragraph 18 refer to Exhibit D4016.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Was it 4016 or 4106?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll double-check that I have the number exactly correct. Sometimes I transpose them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today as were the questions put by members of my team, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. If the members of your team were to put the same questions, the answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender this statement according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And about the associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there are nine unadmitted associated exhibits listed; we're tendering eight of them. Number 00947 is not being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Just with respect to 1D25009, could we only have page 34 because all B/C/S pages have been uploaded and I think we only need the page that the witness has referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit this 92 ter statement as well as eight associated exhibits. Shall we assign the number for the statement first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement receives Exhibit D4077, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the other numbers for the associated exhibits will be assigned in due course by the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out, in the English language, a brief summary of Mr. Andjelko Grahovac's statement. [In English] Andjelko Grahovac was an MP in the BH parliament between 1990 and 1992, and later a member of the Assembly of the Serbian People. He was elected in the Banja Luka municipality. In May 1990, Andjelko Grahovac's wife was threatened whilst pushing a pram containing their daughter. A man approached the pram, had pulled out two knives pointing them at the child's chest. He then said, "This is only the beginning for you." This act was committed in an attempt to make Andjelko Grahovac give up his political engagements; however, he did not. As a result of the multi-party elections, a coalition was created. The Assembly was run in a democratic and tolerant manner with compromises sought to avoid conflicts. A rift among the parties occurred after the decision of the Muslims and Croats to secede from Yugoslavia. The Assembly of the Serbian people was established on 24th of October, 1991, and Momcilo Krajisnik was elected as the first president, whilst he continued to hold the office of president of the Assembly of BH until the beginning of the war. The plebiscite of the Serbian people was held in November 1991, and over 90 per cent of the Serbian people who took part favoured remaining within Yugoslavia. The Serbian people responded to the mobilisation of the JNA as it was a legal duty and they believed that the JNA would protect them, in the case of an attack - people joined in an attempt to prevent the war occurring. At this time, Muslims and Croats were preparing paramilitary forces, including the Green Berets, Handzar division, and the Ustasha paramilitary ZNG, Zbor Narodne Garde. Andjelko Grahovac was aware that the HDZ from Bosnia and Herzegovina were sending Croatian and Muslim volunteers to the battle-fields in Croatia during 1991 where Croatia fought against Serbs. To avoid any future problems, the Assembly of the Serbian people accepted the Cutileiro Plan. The Muslims are responsible for the collapse of the Cutileiro Plan. Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik never promoted the hatred of other peoples; rather, their positions were much more moderate than those of other deputies. The Banja Luka Crisis Staff was established in May 1992. Andjelko Grahovac never received any instructions or orders for the persecution, murder, genocide, ethnic cleansing of other peoples from the area, nor was any persecution or ethnic cleansing planned. It was impossible to communicate with the republican leadership or contact them as the corridor towards Serbia did not exist. Local members of the SDS petitioned Predrag Radic for a long time to accept the post of president of the Municipal Assembly in Banja Luka. He was afraid to accept this position and in general to be a member of the SDS because he did not know what would happen if the elections -- in the elections and feared political retributions by the communists if they were to re-take power; however, he did take the position. Andjelko Grahovac was elected president of the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina in May 1991. The existing ZOBK institution was used as it had been legally founded in the existing system. The ZOBK was established to gain economic independence from Sarajevo and put up political resistance to the separatist policy of the SDA and the HDZ. However, funding for the ZOBK was a constant issue because there was no stable source of income. The ZOBK had little power as the real political and economic power was held by the presidents of Municipal Assemblies. Dr. Karadzic was against the unification of the two Krajinas (in Croatia and in Bosnia), as he saw it as a potential pretext for war. Krajina then became an independent state, gaining economic independence. The SDS had a poor rating in Banja Luka and the Krajina. He was also aware of the roadblocks that had been set up around BH. Andjelko Grahovac visited Manjaca camp for prisoners of war. Whilst visiting he established that the prisoners were safe and that the rules and regulations were respected there. If it was determined there was no evidence to prosecute, the prisoners would be released. As director of the Univerzal company, Andjelko Grahovac only dismissed employees who did not come to work five days in a row without giving any reason. No one was fired for being Muslim or Croat. The situation in Banja Luka during the war was difficult for Serbs as well as for Muslims and Croats because Serbs experienced thefts [sic]. Andjelko Grahovac and his wife received threats over this period. Around this area there were many dangerous people who were responsible for much of the evil that was perpetrated. That was the summary. At the moment, I do not have additional questions for Mr. Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. As you have noted, Mr. Grahovac, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Grahovac, you pointed out in your written evidence that you weren't a member of the ARK Crisis Staff, and I just want to get you to confirm that not only were you not a member, you didn't attend a single session of their meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: That's right. When I was replaced from the position of prime minister of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina in December 1991, officially in the beginning of January 1992, I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. And later on, I did not attend sessions of that body.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And actually, you didn't even know who its members were until sometime in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I knew of some members of the Crisis Staff because they were members of the Crisis Staff ex officio. For example, Vojo Kupresanin, the president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina; or Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, then perhaps the commander of the Krajina Corps and the president of the city Assembly; but the other members, seven, eight, nine, or ten of them, I didn't know them until that point in time, the one that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And really, after your dismissal in January 1992, you really distanced yourself from politics, didn't you? You really focused on running your company and football because of your position with the Borac football club; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a bit angry because of the dishonourable dismissal from that position. I was angry at the political echelons at the time, and since I was rather young at the time, this caused quite a bit of stress. That is why I devoted myself to the company that I worked in, to production, and also I was president of the board's football club. We had a football league then in the Republic of Serbia because we were the only club that had remained in the federal premier league and that's basically what I did during those seven or eight months.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you didn't go to a single ARK Assembly session, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did not attend these sessions of the Assembly because I wasn't a member of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina and I was not a member of any other body of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for a long time, you didn't even attend RS Assembly sessions, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. For a while, precisely because of that situation that I was in, I did not attend sessions of the Assembly of the RS; but at one point in time, I cannot say exactly when, I did join the activities of the Assembly of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But -- and that dismissal -- actually, that completely eliminated you from that circle involving Dr. Karadzic, the other RS leaders and officials of the ARK, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, after the dismissal that's the way it was until I joined in the work of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and later on the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But in 1992 from -- actually, from your dismissal all the way through 1992, you were really out of the political sphere, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot say that a person is totally out of the political sphere -- well, as for influence, no, I didn't really have much influence then. But in the context of what was happening in Banja Luka and Republika Srpska at the time, a person had to be in this whirlpool, whether one liked to or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grahovac, you've actually met with the Office of the Prosecutor's representatives a couple of times in the past, in 2001 and again in 2010. And --

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I met with these representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And in 2001 you told my former colleagues that you knew -- because, nevertheless, you were living in Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992, you knew that hundreds of small businesses belonging to non-Serbs were blown up at night in Banja Luka. That's what you told them; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, just as I spoke about all the other things that I knew because I lived in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also told them you didn't agree with that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also told my former colleagues that you were aware that thousands of Muslims and Croats were evicted from their apartments, sometimes by creating fear in them and sometimes by people breaking into their apartments and throwing them out of their apartments in Banja Luka. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, I did not agree with that because I thought that we Serbs were supposed to fight to defend ourselves from the spectre of the Ustasha ideology among the Croats and Muslims rather than fight for the property of others. However, the situation was such that people did actually do that. But one has to put oneself into the context of that time. I don't think that these were orders coming from a higher level. Quite simply, it was like an epidemic that was rampant among the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And during this same interview in 2001, you were asked by my former colleague, Mr. Inayat, that -- you were asked: "If the Crisis Staff had really wanted, couldn't they have instructed the army and the police to ensure that such things don't happen in Banja Luka?" And you said: "Sure, they could have ..." That's what you said at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. I also said that for a while, while General Vukovic was the commander of the 1st Corps or the 1st Krajina Corps, order was established and the situation was much better than the situation in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact, talking about the Crisis Staff, you also told my colleagues they tolerated these criminal activities, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they actually tolerated that or could not resolve that problem. I would like to point out that -- well, it's not that I'm defending them or justifying what they did. I just wish to explain to this Court, and I'm offering an explanation in the context of those times, wishes were one thing and the reality on the ground and the possibilities that one had were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you remember, Mr. Grahovac, that my colleagues asked you some questions, some specific questions, about Radoslav Brdjanin. And in that interview they asked you whether he talked about a percentage of Muslims and Croats who would be allowed to stay in the Bosanska Krajina and the rest would leave. And your answer was that you heard from one of your Muslim neighbours that he talked about such percentages. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said then, although I had not heard that directly from Mr. Brdjanin. So I actually received this information from the colleague who worked with me and who was still in Banja Luka in 1991, 1992, 1993 was involved in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Mr. Inayat asked you what percentage he talked about, and your answer to him was: "I don't know really, but probably a minimum percentage in order to show how Serb he is ..." And you also said that he said those things because of Karadzic and Krajisnik and to show how he is a big nationalist or Serb or patriot. That's what you said about Mr. Brdjanin during your audio-recorded interview with the OTP in 2001; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I would like to say that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in their statements never said anything about percentages or the expulsion of other peoples. I said this in the context of Mr. Brdjanin's nature and his mind-set. Quite simply, he liked to figure prominently, he liked to talk too much, sometimes a bit carelessly too. He did more damage to himself by what he said than by something that he possibly did. Quite simply, he wanted to prove himself before our leadership. It's not that Mr. Karadzic had anything to do with it. He wanted to show that he was the best and the strongest Serb among all of us. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So you're confirming that these were your words at the time in 2001; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could have just five more minutes before we break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll be sitting until 3.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one more brief area before we break for lunch, Mr. Grahovac, and it's about your visit to Manjaca, and you discuss that at paragraph 39 of your statement and that was in the context of your friend Adnan Dzonlic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said in your statement that all prisoners in Manjaca were considered prisoners of war, but your friend Mr. Dzonlic was a civilian, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: In that statement I explained what I had heard about Mr. Dzonlic and how he had arrived in Manjaca. According to what I heard, he had been arrested in a combat area because he wanted to leave Republika Srpska across Slavonia which was a combat area to go to Okucani and then to Croatia.
