He was going to do that through his own means. You know that everybody who was caught in a war-struck area is considered a prisoner of war if they're caught there, and then they are interviewed. And if the investigators establish that they were not guilty, they either proceed with the interrogation or let him go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. I'll re-tell -- I'll quote to you exactly what you said in the interview in 2001 about Mr. Dzonlic. You said: "He wanted to leave Banja Luka and he chose a pretty incredible way to do it. He wanted -- or I think his intention was to leave Banja Luka by escorting a very sick person, very ill person, an invalid or someone like that. He wanted to go," as you've just explained, "he wanted to go through Okucani, through Western Slavonia, to Zagreb. He was found in the war zone and I think because of that -- because of where they found him, they captured him and detained him. As far as I know, he was never, you know, in any of that." And my colleague said: "Never in any?" And then you responded: "Never in any of the fighting, no. His problem was because they found him in the fighting area, the war zone, and you know what that means." So what you were telling my colleagues in 2001 was that Mr. Dzonlic was a civilian; right? He was never in any of the fighting as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Dzonlic had not participated in any kind of fighting. I only know that he was a reserve officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. I believe that he was a tank man. He was not really actively involved in the JNA, but he also wasn't involved with the enemy forces. I had known him from childhood. We went to the same school, to the same university. It was my duty to help him. I emphasise that. I believe that he was indeed a civilian but that he was found in a war zone. You have to put all that in the context of war developments. It is not a comfortable situation. People get killed in such an area for a trifle thing, so nobody really found it easy to believe that he had arrived there as a civilian. That's why he was interrogated and later on he was exchanged. In my explanation, I said that I had tried to get him released. I appealed to Mr. Goran Bijelic, who died about that time, and Mr. Stevilovic, the security chief of the 1st Krajina Corps. In -- strangely enough, during those couple weeks he also got killed en route from -- to Teslic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am having trouble with the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. I reconnected. I had disabled LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, we'll take a break so that could be solved during the break. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 22 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Grahovac, I'd just like to stay with the subject of this Manjaca visit for a few short minutes more and get you to have a look at a document before I ask you the next question. It's 65 ter number 25680. And it's a list of prisoners visited at Manjaca that we recovered from the ministry -- from the Kozara barracks, actually, in Banja Luka. If we go over to page 5 of this document, please, and scroll down to number 235 on the list. There's Mr. Dzonlic's name, Mr. Grahovac, do you see that at 235?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it says that Mr. Dzonlic -- pardon me for the mispronunciation. That Mr. Dzonlic arrived there on 20 May 1992 and he was released or, as you said, exchanged on 14 October 1992. So whatever you may or may not have been able to accomplish, he was there for five months. So what I'd like to put to you, Mr. Grahovac, is actually you don't know for a fact that he was interrogated and, Mr. Grahovac, what I'd like to put to you is that he was never interrogated, he was never investigated because they knew right away there was no reason to interrogate him. Mr. Dzonlic, along with many other men on this list, were held exclusively to be exchanged, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to tell you anything about the reasons why he was kept. All I can tell you is that I tried to get him out of the camp as quickly as possible at the Manjaca camp. There were a lot of people there. As you know, everybody had to be interrogated and after the interrogations, they did what they did with them. But I think that it is good that at the end of the day he was exchanged and that the story ended well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Happily so, but, Mr. Grahovac, you've already said in 1992 you were out of it. So you don't know that people were interrogated at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: As I've told you and as I stated in my statement, I was in communication with the camp warden at Manjaca, Colonel Popovic, who was my in-laws' neighbour. He told me that procedure would be followed to the letter and that the detainees in that camp were in safe hands because they were guarded by the Yugoslav People's Army. All that was left for me to do was to trust him. That's all I could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another area and that's about the unit you discussed at paragraphs 31 and 32 of your statement, and you referred to them as Milankovic's men. That's the same unit, actually, that you used to take over the Kozara transmitter in August 1991, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the same man and the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that unit was allowed to eventually join the army, first, the JNA and later they served as a VRS unit, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that that unit organised itself. It was self-organised, as it were. According to what we believed, it actually wanted to defend the Serbian people from [indiscernible] aggression. I emphasise I would like to explain things to you, and for you to understand things we have to go back --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: -- along the history line and we have to talk about the Second World War and the relationship between --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: -- Croats and Muslims and Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Grahovac, if Dr. Karadzic wants to ask you about that, he can. All I want to ask you about is whether you can confirm that this unit was allowed to eventually join the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I wish to explain the essence and the origin of that unit and how it got incorporated in the military, and I can't do it in just one or two sentences. Allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Grahovac, do you want to answer my question or do you not want to answer my question? It's a simple question. Was it incorporated into the army or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that unit was eventually incorporated into the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact, they were considered an elite unit of the Bosnian Serb army, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to explain. I wanted to tell you what kind of unit they were and how they were organised. I wish to do that, with your permission. Of course it was not the most elite unit of the VRS or of the JNA; however, its members were patriots and they were ready to die for the cause, and the cause was the defence of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you quickly another document, it's P2855, please. Right. The document, Mr. Grahovac, that you see in front of you is dated 28 July 1995 [sic], and for your information it's signed by General Tolimir, and it's a report on paramilitary formations on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So my first question is: In paragraph 1 of this document, that's the top paragraph on the page, you see that among the groups mentioned is a group called Vukovi, that's the same group as that which was led by Milankovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were known by that name, Vukovi, Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go over to page 5 in your language and page 4, I think, of the English translation. So the first full paragraph at the top of the page in your language and the, I think, seventh full paragraph in English says that: "The detachment of Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor has about 150 men and is as of recently formally under the command of the 1 KK and members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting and recently attacked the Tactical Group 3 command post, arresting one army colonel in the process." So that's the same group, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I suppose that it was the same group. I would like to emphasise that there were very frequent conflicts between junior officers and the officers of the JNA because JNA officers were old and hardened communists and certain problems were bound to occur between the two groups. I wouldn't agree that the whole unit was problematic and that they all plundered. We can only talk about individuals and certainly not about the whole unit. I would like to stress that we did not have a choice. We had to stand up against the ZNGs from Zagreb or the Green Berets. We could not use teachers or professors from the university. We had to find a good match for those people. Put everything in the context of war, this is the worst condition that can strike humanity, and I'm emphasising that members of that unit were patriots, they were not all criminals. I would agree with Mr. Karadzic, and I said that in my statement, that those who had been involved in looting should have been brought to trial --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Stop. You don't need to repeat your statement. Thank you. My question to you is: This document shows that even as members of the VRS, members of this unit committed crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Could you please point me to the paragraph, to the part of the document that you're referring to, because I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. In your language go to the first full paragraph at the top of the page, where it says just after it mentions the name of the detachment of Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor, it says: "... members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting ..." That's a crime; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: These were not crimes. Let me emphasise once again. There were conflicts between the officers of the JNA who were pro-communist and those new reserve officers. There was jealousy among people. People competed for the position of the best commander, the best officer. It's a sphere of military philosophy that is hard to understand. Because of conflicts and jealousy, they spread all sorts of rumours. I can't deny and say that there were no lootings or individual thefts, but in general all of our units that were attached to the VRS, their conduct followed all of our rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is yes; correct? Or do you even remember the question?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I do remember the question, and I would like to reiterate that you cannot label everything as looting and especially you cannot link that to the whole unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, but you said that through 1992 you were out of it. That's why I just asked you a question about what the document says on its face. So on its face this document reports members of that unit being involved in criminal activity, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: If that's on the face of the document, that's the document. The only question is who the author of the document is and what his intentions were. I tried to explain to you what the situation was at that time in the units of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. I'd like you to look at a short film clip now. It's P3001. And I think it's been synchronised, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, Your Honours, I wonder if my colleagues in the AV booth can do something about turning up the sound, because as I know from following the proceedings this is about the third time we've been unable to play things in Sanction with sound. And if it can't be solved immediately, we'll have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may just pause for a couple of seconds, Your Honour, because I come very close to the end of my cross-examination, to see if this can be fixed very quickly, with your permission. Now, rather than interrupt the flow of proceedings anymore, Your Honour, I'd just like to move on to the next area, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful. If we could just go ahead with this video-clip which is P3001, please. And thank you to my colleagues, this is clearly resolving a problem that has been of some long standing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: Fifth anniversary of 'Vukovi sa Vucijaka." Momcilo Krajisnik, the speaker of the Assembly and the SDS candidate for the Presidency, addressed the audience. "Momcilo Krajisnik: You from 'Vukovi' from Vucijak who are present here today in civilian clothes rather than in uniforms, you belong to this area as much as you belong to people of Dalmatian, Lika, Western Slavonia, Posavina. Your war path is difficult but glorious. Since 1991 when you burned the candle of freedom defending the people of the Serbian Krajina, you went through all the theatres of war and participated in many combats in Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Both your friends and enemies will remember you for your heroism. You and your legendary commander Veljko Milankovic are history's favourites. I have no doubt ... I have no doubt that children in schools, and especially military school cadets, will ask themselves when studying about our combat - which formation did 'Wolves of Vucijak belong to. The response will be: It was the unit every army in the world would be proud of. Your deeds are immortal because each of you is worth two men. In other words, we can say that you belonged to the entire Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik here in this video-clip is talking about the same group that General Tolimir was talking about in the paragraph that I read to you from P2855 and that's the same group you used in the take-over of the Kozara transmitter in August 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have one last question, in paragraph 22 of your statement, your written evidence, you said that Dr. Karadzic was vehemently opposed to the establishment of a Krajina state. And, Mr. Grahovac, the fact that Dr. Karadzic was opposed was determinative, wasn't it, the fact of his opposition determined the issue; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. First of all, does it relate to the Republic of Serbian Krajina or does it refer to our own Krajina, to the former Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I formulated my question based on what you wrote in your statement, and you wrote that Dr. Karadzic was vehemently opposed to the establishment of a Krajina state. It never happened, did it? A Krajina state never happened; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: You're right, but only if you have in mind the state of Krajina that would have consisted of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the association of municipalities of Krajina. It never took off the ground because we actually opted for the integration of all of our Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It never took off the ground because of Dr. Karadzic's intervention; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: No, not only of Dr. Karadzic's intervention, but also some people in Krajina who did not want that and I suppose of the entire leadership at a higher level. They had more information and they were able to reach a decision that was in the interest of the entire Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just, before we close, want to show you a document. It's P5452. All right. These are the minutes of the 14th ARK Assembly from 29th February 1992, and at this Assembly, 168 -- out of a total of 168 Assemblymen, 151 showed up and also attending were Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Professor Koljevic, and Mr. Ostojic. And if you see that, then I'd like to go over to page 2 in both languages, please. There's only two items on the agenda and the second one is the statute of the ARK in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, in respect to item 2, you see in your language in the middle of the page and at the bottom of page 2, Dr. Karadzic stressing that: "It would be a crime against the Krajina if it were declared a republic. Those who advocate such childish ideas are exposing the Serbian people to trouble. The Bosnian Krajina doesn't need, he said, any National Councils, since it has legally elected organs and the republican Serbian authorities are fully functioning ..." And after debate, if you go over to page 3 in English but stay at the bottom of B/C/S. After debate, the Krajina deputies accepted the constitution of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina and concluded that the status of the ARK would be incorporated into the constitution of the Republic of Serbian People with 141 deputy -- 148 deputies actually in agreement and no opposition whatsoever. So this is Dr. Karadzic coming to a meeting of the Krajina Assembly determining the issue. It was put to bed here once and for all, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: To be honest, I see this document for the first time because obviously this was done in a period when I was not really very active in politics. I would agree here with Mr. Karadzic, that these were really infantile ideas on the part of some people. Because we needed more integration, we needed more unity rather than be divided into small parochial communes. I think the arguments advanced by Mr. Karadzic and his associates - although I emphasise that I wasn't present at this session - were powerful and it's probable that the deputies of the session voted for.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's Dr. Karadzic determining the issue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: You can't put it that way. In the Assembly of Republika Srpska, later when I attended the sessions, there was always a democratic debate on all issues. It's a different matter that in some situations Mr. Karadzic's arguments were strong enough to prevail. We have to remember that he was the greatest authority for us and he had the best ideas and the best solutions for all issues crucial to the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two or three questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grahovac, while we have this document before us and while we are discussing the suggestion that I determined the outcome of this session, could you tell us, did I have any instruments, any tools to push through my political will? Did I punish or expel people or did I just win them over by the strength of my arguments?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I think I can be very objective on this issue. You know that sometimes we saw things differently on certain political issues, but it is true that the strongest political arguments won the day in the end. You did not have any instruments of power to make people, to force people, to accept your views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You began to talk about the reasons for self-organisation, that's on page 58, and you recalled the barbaric behaviour of the Muslims and the Ustashas during the Second World War. Could you complete that thought? And you were talking about how it came about that the Wolves organised themselves?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I had indeed started to talk about that. The barbaric acts of the Muslims and Ustashas, especially in the Second World War, brought out the worst in the masses and I'll give you a few examples beginning with my own personal example and later citing some general ones. From my earliest childhood, I heard from my parents, my grandmother, I heard horrible stories about the sufferings of our ancestors. My grandmother, Ljuba, lost her two sons to Ustasha hands, Veljko and Rada. My uncle who lived in Novi Grad municipality was found left for dead by the Ustashas and my grandmother took him in and raised him as her own son --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there are many things concerning the concentration camps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to tell us you joined the Wolves because of those facts? I'm not following where are we going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain if you let me. The thing is that people were aware what had happened in the Second World War and they didn't dare to and didn't want to allow that situation to be repeated, wherein a hundred Serbs would be taken to be slaughtered by one Ustasha. To this day there is a cemetery in Mirogoj with the graves of 842 children, children who were killed in the only concentration camp for children that ever existed in the world. That was the Jastrebarsko camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard enough about this. If you could -- would like to add anything specifically with respect to the Wolves, but otherwise please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell us, why did people not rely on the federal state and the JNA to protect them and why did they self-organise instead into the Wolves and other groups?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: We had thought that the JNA would take our Serbian side, but in fact it didn't happen that way. In practice, there were a lot of communists among the top JNA cadre, including General Uzelac, who was too busy doing less-important things, so that the people had to organise themselves, had to take things into their own hands, and had to defend themselves from another genocide. That was the reason for all these units that had organised themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: His Excellency, the Presiding Judge, asked you if that was the reason why you joined the Wolves. Were you a member of the Wolves or did you just defend them inasmuch as they were not criminals?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Wolves. I was a man who was politically active and of course I supported all the patriotic forces that participated in the defence of the Serbian people, and of course I was in favour of punishing all those who were responsible for looting and other crimes. Certainly I was not a member of the Wolves from Vucijak and I don't deserve to be given such an honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 61 it was put to you that there had been buildings blown up, break-ins, looting, et cetera. How did the authorities view that? How did they react? And did the Muslims and Croats report these things to the authorities? How did the authorities treat these crimes?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: To be frank, I don't know how the local authorities in these places where it happened acted, but from the few examples that I know, I believe that many prominent people, people who hold high offices in Bosnia-Herzegovina now should be here instead of you and they were pursuing their own interests. That's the reason why our just cause was tarnished, because many people put their own personal interests before the interests of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case that Muslims and Croats remained to live during the war in Banja Luka normally; and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I think Banja Luka can actually be proud that the greatest percentage of Muslims and Croats remained there. Those who joined our army were respected members of the community, and I remember there was a man, a Croat, Tonce [phoen] Ruzic, who worked as the deputy of our municipality. In my company there were at least 10, 15 Muslims and Croats and there -- in my unit, my infantry unit, there were also about 10 and 15 Muslims and Croats who fought together with us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Grahovac. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you didn't tender the list of prisoners visited at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, there was no need, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson, it's about the scheduling next year after the winter recess. We'll resume on the 16th, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erceg. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Erceg.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us speak slowly, both of us, and between questions and answers we need to make a short pause. If you look at the transcript, pay attention to the cursor, that means the interpretation is finished. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D9530.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement faithfully reflect what you have stated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would your answers be substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Essentially, they would be the same, but not verbatim because of the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this 92 ter statement, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, if you could explain us about the associated exhibits you are tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're tendering 41 associated exhibits. One of them is not on our 65 ter list and we would ask that it be added. It was left off due to oversight and that's 05453. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there are several documents that have been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are, although I believe that the 41 that I referred to are the ones that are not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D9856 referred to in para 27, I take it that has been admitted as Exhibit D3970; and 1D9859 referred to in para 40 was admitted as Exhibit D4036; and 1D9882 referred to in para 82 was admitted as D4057; and 1D9886 referred to in para 96 was admitted as Exhibit D4044; and 1D9887 referred to in para 97 was admitted as Exhibit D4050; and 65 ter 5453 referred to in para 39 was admitted as Exhibit D4035; and 65 ter 5831 referred to in para 24 was admitted Exhibit D4015; and finally, 65 ter number 17188 referred to in para 45 was admitted as Exhibit D4037. And I'm not sure whether the English translation was 65 ter 15075 referred to in para 90 was English translation of 65 ter 1575 referred to in para 90 was uploaded. There seems to be some duplication in 1D9874 referred to in para 64, I'm referring to the English translations. So if the Defence could check it later on. Otherwise, do you have any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So -- except for those that have been already admitted, the Rule 92 ter statement as well as the associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence. Shall we assign the number for the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement receives Exhibit D4086, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The other numbers will be assigned in due course by the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I will now read out a short summary of Mr. Erceg's statement in English. [In English] At the municipal and regional level, Mr. Nikola Erceg held the following positions: Member of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party; a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka; in March 1992, president of the Executive Committee of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; in May 1992, member of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; member of the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka municipality; member of the Banja Luka commission for the collection of food for the Army of Republika Srpska. Towards the end of July 1995, Nikola Erceg was appointed as a member of the War Presidency of the municipality of Banja Luka. Furthermore, on the republican and federal level, Nikola Erceg performed the duties of a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo and in the Assembly of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in Belgrade after the first multi-party elections in 1990; then a deputy in the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina after its establishment in October 1991; in the second half of 1992, Mr. Erceg was a minister for industry and energy in the Government of Republika Srpska; in September 1992, deputy chairman of the legislative commission of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska; in April 1993, a member of the legislative committee of the Assembly of Republika Srpska; in May 1993, a member of the board of the National Bank of Republika Srpska. Nikola Erceg worked also as a director of the electricity supply company of Republika Srpska. Nikola Erceg never became familiar with Variants A and B plans and their content. In those times, the Serbs' main intention was to remain in a joint state of Yugoslavia. The ARK Assembly adopted a decision to form an ARK Crisis Staff, headed by Brdjanin. The Crisis Staff became the main body of ARK. The ARK Crisis Staff had no jurisdiction over the police, nor could it issue orders to the army, which had its own chain of command. After the ARK Crisis Staff was established, the Executive Committee continued with its regular sessions, but no longer on a daily basis. Nikola Erceg was not aware of the reason why the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was renamed to War Staff, nor if there were any instructions issued from Pale regarding the members of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff or any rules of procedure therein. There was a rift between the Sarajevo option and the Krajina option because the Banja Luka intellectuals were in favour of establishing a state that would comprise the two Krajinas (Bosnian and Croatian), which was opposed by the Sarajevo option led by Karadzic. With the outbreak of war, Pale was unable to exert control over Serbian communities, which prompted the establishment of a regional government, for example, in Banja Luka, because it was impossible to communicate with Pale due to the simple fact that all communication lines were severed and no regular contacts could be maintained. Mr. Nikola Erceg was not content with the co-operation between certain municipal organs and his office. Some municipalities demonstrated a high degree of independence because they were economically strong. The ARK was unable to control municipalities like Prijedor. It was up to the municipalities to accept or reject the decisions of the ARK in spite of the ARK Crisis Staff decisions that all ARK Crisis Staff decisions were binding for the municipal organs in the ARK. Nikola Erceg was present at the ARK Crisis Staff meetings when the existence of Omarska and Keraterm was mentioned, but all they discussed with the municipal representatives was logistical support and the financing of those centres. Manjaca was discussed at the ARK Crisis Staff meetings in the same context. The ARK policy was not aimed at a violent or any other form of expulsion or persecution of the non-Serb population, and so the ARK Crisis Staff adopted few decisions and conclusions in that respect. The Banja Luka municipality Assembly, SO, which had Muslims -- Muslim and Croatian representatives, paid attention to the ownership of property, and so properties belonging to those who had left Banja Luka were given for temporary use and an inventory was made of all belongings and their condition so that they could be returned intact to their rightful owners. While working as a director of the Electricity Supply Company of Republika Srpska, Nikola Erceg witnessed problems concerning power cuts on a daily basis in households in Banja Luka. However, that did not attract as much attention as Sarajevo. He himself did not have electricity in the centre of Banja Luka for 40 days at a time. And at the moment, I do not have additional questions for Mr. Erceg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, although I understand this is your first time testifying here it the Tribunal, you gave statements, that is, interviews, that were taped in 2001 and 2002 to representatives of the Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And indeed, portions of those interviews comprise parts of your current statement before this Court?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I therefore presume that your position is that you were telling the truth during those interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 74 of the statement that you saw a few moments ago on the screen - and, Mr. Erceg, if at any time you need a hard copy of that statement, I think it can be provided for you or we can call it up on the screen - but at paragraph 74 you state: "It is clear that everyone had the right to their property even after moving out." Now, in fact, Mr. Erceg, you don't really know much about this at all and you don't know, really, whether people had the right to their property or not. And you even acknowledged that in your own statement at a later portion. That's the case, isn't it? You don't know much about this issue and you admitted it in your statement at paragraph 85?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 39 of your statement, you state that the ARK Crisis Staff was established on the 5th of May, 1992, and you also state that this was "in accordance with the instructions from Pale ..." But then you go on to explain that characterisation in accordance by saying that you meant that it was possible that somebody misconstrued those instructions from Pale. Previously, however, during your 2001 interview you stated instead that the -- for example, the position which was asserted by the ARK Crisis Staff in a conclusion of 26 May 1992, where it was stated by the ARK Crisis Staff that the decisions of the staff are binding for all Crisis Staffs in the municipalities, was "the consequence of the document issued by the president of the RS government, Mr. Djeric ..." That's found at 1D9896 at e-court page 36. That's your 2001 interview. You're welcome to see it, but if you can -- you may be able to confirm in any event that that was the position you took when you were asked about this issue in 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just ask honourable Mr. Tieger, what -- what statement he is using?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He referred to 39 -- but it should be 38 of his statement, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That may be that you're right. We'll get to the reason I'm misnumbering that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I apologise for that, and I'll try to watch the particular numbers, maybe have my colleague double-check as I recite them. So thank you for that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Erceg. I think the substance was clear enough, but I'll try to be precisely accurate about the numbers of the paragraphs. So my -- my question was with regard to the portion of your statement where you said that the establishment of the ARK Crisis Staff on the 5th of May, 1992, was in accordance with the instructions from Pale, but your further comment in this current statement that it was -- you said that because it was possible that someone misconstrued the instructions for Pale. I'm now confronting you with what you said in 2001, where you noted that, for example, that the conclusion of the ARK Crisis Staff on the 26th of May that its decisions were binding, was in your words "the consequence of the document issued by the president of the RS government, Mr. Djeric ..." And I was simply asking you, if you were able to do so, to confirm that that is indeed the position you took in 2001 when you were interviewed by representatives of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether I was correctly interpreted; however, I know that at the time there was a great deal of confusion about that. I personally thought that the Crisis Staff should not have been established at the level of the ARK Krajina, since that had to do with each and every municipality. As for this fact whether or not there were requests from Pale for them to be established, this is what the confusion was all about. At first, we did not have any written instructions from Prime Minister Djeric. Roughly, it turned out on the basis of stories that this was supposed to be done, there were instructions coming from Sarajevo -- no, from Pale to have that done. I think that after a while this instruction from Djeric did arrive, and on the basis of that I understood that I was right; namely, that the Krajina should not have been established -- I mean, not the Krajina, the Crisis Staff of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in that case I would tender page 36 of 1D9896, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn also --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, let the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we assign a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P6528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly, I'd like to turn to what you said in 2002 to the representatives of the Tribunal, this time at pages 45 through 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 1D09895.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the context here again, Mr. Erceg, and I can go back several pages to show you the specific reference to the May 5th, 1992, date on which -- which you referred to previously and which is reflected in your statement for the founding of the Crisis Staff. But in 2002 this issue was raised with you and you said the following. First of all, at page -- start on page 45, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It should start -- should start toward the bottom of that page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say -- you were asked: "Can you name the people who were appointed to the Crisis Staff?" And then the answer is not heard. The question is: "You told us that you issued this decision as a result of orders from Pale." And then the clarification: "That a Crisis Staff be formed ..." That's your remarks to the interpreter, the question is asked: "Who picked the people who were to be on this Crisis Staff?" And then it continues and there's some inaudibles: "Q. Did someone else tell him to choose the people we see in the next page?" And then we see in the middle of the page: "I think it might have been Brdjanin." The question was asked: "Who gave you the names to put into this decision? "A. I think it might have been Brdjanin, I don't know. Someone gave it to me, I know that I didn't comprise these names by myself. "Q. So the orders came from Pale that there was to be a Crisis Staff formed and Brdjanin gave you the names of the people." You say: "I believe it was Brdjanin ... and the contents of this document is purely in format, it is prepared according to that which was issued from Pale. "And how did you receive the orders from Pale, do you remember?" You were asked. And you say: "I don't know, usually let's say it would come via Brdjanin himself, I asked him on paper and he says yes, on paper. "Q. Again, so the orders that came from Pale would come via Brdjanin?" And you said: "I'm talking just about this specifically." And "this specifically" as we saw was the instruction from Pale describing the Crisis Staff. So contrary to what you now say in paragraph 37 about receiving no instructions regarding the membership of the Crisis Staff and contrary to the position you take in paragraph 39 that the establishment of the Crisis Staff in accordance with instructions for Pale only meant that somebody misconstrued the Djeric instructions, the fact is that when you first discussed this issue more than ten years ago, much closer to the events in question, you stated that these -- that the establishment of the Crisis Staff, as reflected on the May 5th document, was pursuant to instructions from Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: That's the way it should be, but I'm not sure because at first there were no instructions sort of and then this instruction appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I didn't want to interrupt before the witness answered. I give him a lot of credit for answering that question directly, but to me that question is extremely hard to follow. It practically takes up a page of transcript, and I think it would be better in the future if Mr. Tieger could break up his questions so it's easier for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, yes -- but, Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- from his 2002 interview, did you find a passage where the witness said the orders came from Pale? I read Madam Korner's questions, but I'm not sure whether I read the answer confirming the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, here's one. A question was: "So the orders came from Pale that there was to be a" -- this is page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We start from 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bottom. "So the orders that came from Pale would come via Brdjanin ..." Yes, start from there, yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Right. "I believe it was Brdjanin and the contents of this document is purely in format, it is prepared according to that which was issued from Pale." Then he's asked: "How did you receive the orders ... ?" He says: "I don't know, usually let's say it would come via Brdjanin himself, I asked him on paper and he said yes on paper. "So the orders that came from Pale would come via Brdjanin?" And he said: "I'm talking just about this specifically." So he reduced the discussion to this [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All we heard is that he referred to Brdjanin: "I believe it was Brdjanin ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not following your question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the order came from Pale --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "So the orders that came from Pale," which is the subject of this discussion. Did you get orders from Pale? And he said previous it was prepared according to that which was issued from Pale, that is the membership [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the question and his answer was: "I believe it was Brdjanin ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the question was: "The orders came from Pale that there was to be a Crisis Staff formed and Brdjanin gave you the names of the people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. "A. I believe it was Brdjanin ... and the contents of this document," meaning the May 5th document, "is purely in format. It is prepared according to that which was issued from Pale." And then the question was: "And how did you receive the orders from Pale ..." And he said: "I don't know, usually ... let's say it would come via Brdjanin himself ..." And then the question was: "So the orders that came from Pale would come via Brdjanin?" And the answer was: "Well, I'm talking just about this specifically." So this focused on the subject matter at hand which was the relationship between the 5 May 1992 document that he prepared and the instructions from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I would tender those pages, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them as Exhibit P6529.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that particular permutation of the Crisis Staff that was reflected in the May 5 document that was recorded there by you -- well, Mr. Erceg, you were aware that an ARK Crisis Staff or regional Crisis Staff has been in existence since at least February 1992; correct? I believe you were asked about that as well in your previous interview.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know whether it was before the month of May. In Sarajevo, Izetbegovic, they did form a Crisis Staff at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. If we can turn to 1D9896, your 2001 interview and turn to page 42, toward the bottom, please. Were you asked: "Who established the ARK Crisis Staff? Who was it established by?" You said: "All the -- all the instructions, decisions that managed to find their way to the ARK, they needed to be formalised. They needed to have -- because of their own accord they couldn't become legally binding in any way but." The question was asked: "So you're saying that you formalised, what was the informal arrangement for the first four months of 1992 or for the first five months of 1992 in that document dated 5 May 1992?" Your answer was: "Well, it did not really function in the early months but this, this was made formal, this formalised the whole. Maybe it did function as far as the individual actions by many of the people involved, yes. But the actual formal decision of establishing the Crisis Staff was this one, this is when it was made formal." So, first of all, those were your -- that was your position in 2001 when you were asked about the Crisis Staff that was reflected in the May 5th document and about the existence of a Crisis Staff that preceded it; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: May I say something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I don't understand this at all. Nothing had to be formalised. And in the meantime, I believe that it was in March, the Executive Council of the ARK was set up in order to do whatever it was supposed to do. It was only in May, on the 5th of May, that the Crisis Staff was set up. Everything that was done up to then was formalised through the work of the Executive Council of the ARK. At the moment when the Crisis Staff was set up, the Crisis Staff gradually took over all the things and authorities that were supposed to be continued through the Executive Council. The Executive Council gradually faded out and the Crisis Staff was gradually more and more activated in various spheres of life. Now, whether that had to be formalised with some kind of a decision, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, no, I think you're focusing on something quite different. I had asked you about the Crisis Staff referred to in the 5 May document and about the existence of a Crisis Staff before and asked you to confirm or dispute the position you took in 2001. So I'd like to now tender those pages, pages 42 and 43, and show you one additional document related to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, we'll add those two pages to Exhibit P6528.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I call up 65 ter 05415, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What you'll see coming up on the screen, Mr. Erceg, is a decision of the 24th of February, 1992, from the SDS Executive Committee signed by Mr. Dukic, appointing Mr. Vukic as co-ordinator for SAO Krajina, and listing his duties which include, as you can see in the third entry under number 2: "To take part in the work of the SAO Krajina Crisis Staff ..." Now, that, sir, is a reflection of the existence of an SAO Krajina Crisis Staff as of that date, a Crisis Staff which you referred to when you were interviewed in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: So why was the decision on the setting up of the Crisis Staff issued on the 5th of May if this thing was in effect at the same time? I believe that this was at the republican level, I assume, but I'm not sure. And if this was the basis for the work of the Crisis Staff, why did we formalise the Crisis Staff of the ARK only three months later with a decision of the Executive Council? It doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Erceg, at paragraph 22 of your current statement you say that the Autonomous Region of Krajina was formed at the outbreak of the war because it was impossible to communicate with Pale due to the fact that all communication lines were severed and no regular contact could be made. Similarly at paragraph 34 you state that the lack of communication with Pale was the reason for forming ARK institutions. Now, first of all, Mr. Erceg, the plain reality is that the ARK -- the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, was established months before the outbreak of the conflict and any alleged communication difficulties; correct? In fact, it was established on the 16th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's call up P3421, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a decision on the proclamation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina as an inseparable part of the federal state of federative Yugoslavia. It describes what is intended to be some of the territory -- what is and is intended to be some of the territory. It states in Article 5 that: "The Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina will reach a temporary decision on the government ... and the organisation ...," et cetera. And if we look to the end of the document, we'll see the date of its issuance in Banja Luka as 16 September 1991. And it's signed by Mr. Kupresanin. This was the transformation, the transition, from the ZOBK into the Autonomous Region of Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG
utterances.text: This document, while the federal state of Yugoslavia was still alive, and I don't mean that it lived as a state, it was in the stage of disintegration and this was produced in order to calm down the situation, to regenerate the state, and to provide conditions conducive to political activities. So this is not the same ARK which was established due to war activities on the ground and as a result of the fact that life had to be organised on the ground. These are two totally different terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm moving into a slightly different topic which certainly can't be covered in the few minutes left. It may be better to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I could return to one associated exhibit issue, it's number 15075, and this was one that the translation wasn't available to the Chamber. But in fact we had asked the OTP to upload the translation and by mistake they hadn't done it. But they've done it now. So I would ask the Chamber if it would look at that document and if it believes that it's an inseparable part of the statement to also admit it as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a look. We shall adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning. Mr. Erceg, I would like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving evidence at The Hague. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
